sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Nt** ​(*neith*) — ‌Weaving, War, ‌the Primeval ​Waters ​· Water, ​the terrifying ​one — ​belongs to ‌the ​Egyptian tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Weaving, War, ‌Hunting". The ​name means ​"Water, ​the terrifying ​one"[^1].

**Nt** ​— Neith ‌— ​is Egypt’s ‌primordial goddess: ​older than ‌the ​Ennead, mistress ‌of the ​arrows of ‌war and ​the ​loom of ‌creation, who ‌wove the ‌world’s ​fabric at ​Sais before ‌the gods ​had names. ​The ‌ancients called ​her “the ​great cow ‌who ​bore the ‌sun”, and ​made her ​the ​mother of ​Sobek, of ‌the crocodiles, ‌and of ​Ra ‌himself in ​the oldest ​cosmogonic strand.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Nt** ​and serves ‌its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/neith/). ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*neith* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓈖𓏏𓋌**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"Water, ​the terrifying ​one"[^1].

‌The ​canonical ‌spelling ​**Nt** matches ‌the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*neith* contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ​is ‌claimed. ‌The ‌editorial ​work is ​to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ‌and provenance, ​and ‌keep ​the ​original evidence ​visible. ​The ‌displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a ​description ‌computed from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**n** → ‌**N** ​— ​Same
- ​**e** → ‌**—** ​— ​Vowel ​not written
- ‌**i** ​→ ‌**—** ​— ‌Vowel not ​written
- ‌**t** ‌→ ​**t** — ​Same
- ​**h** ​→ ‌**—** — ‌Not ​written

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/ˈneɪɪθ/ ​(conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading ​— ‌Egyptian vocalisation ​not ‌attested.[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- ​**N-** ​— ​Written nt ​or ‌n.t; ​conventionally ‌vocalised ​“Neith”.
- ‌**-t** ​— ‌Feminine ending; ​the ‌name ​may ​be ‌a ‌participle, ‌“the ​terrible one” ​or ‌“the ​weaver”.
- ​**N.t** ‌— ​The ​dot ‌in the ​transliteration ‌marks ​the ​feminine ​ending ​written ‌with ‌the water-ripple: ​the ‌goddess’s ​name ​carries ‌her ‌own ‌element.

‌For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ​approximation ‌is: ​“NAY-ith”

​Kindred and ​historical ‌forms ​of ​the ​name:

- ‌**Greek** ​— ‌Νηΐθ (Nēïth)

​One ‌of ​Egypt’s ‌oldest ‌attested ​theonyms ​— ​her sign ​appears ‌on ‌Predynastic ​pottery.

sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Nt** ​— Neith ‌— ‌is Egypt’s ​primordial goddess: ​older ​than the ​Ennead, ​mistress of ‌the ​arrows of ​war ‌and the ​loom of ‌creation, ​who wove ‌the ​world’s fabric ​at ​Sais before ​the ​gods had ‌names. The ​ancients ‌called her ​“the ‌great cow ​who ‌bore the ​sun”, ‌and made ​her the ​mother ‌of Sobek, ‌of ‌the crocodiles, ​and ​of Ra ‌himself ​in the ​oldest cosmogonic ‌strand.[^1]

### ​The Weaver

​Creator ‌as textile-worker: ​she ‌wove the ​world’s ​fabric on ​her loom ​at ‌Sais.

### Mistress ‌of ​the Bow

‌War-goddess ​whose arrows ​decide ‌battles; her ‌symbol is ‌the ‌crossed arrows ​on ‌a shield.

### ​Mother ​of the ​Gods

‌Sole parent ​of Sobek ​in ​the Fayum ‌tradition; ​in the ​Esna ​theology she ‌bears ​the sun.

### ‌Lady of ​Sais

‌Her city ​in ‌the western ‌Delta ​held her ​great ​temple and ​the mysteries ‌of ‌the primeval ​waters.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Nt ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Weaver** ​— ​Creator ‌as ​textile-worker: ‌she ​wove ‌the ​world’s ‌fabric on ​her ‌loom ​at ​Sais.
- ‌**Mistress ‌of ‌the ​Bow** ​— ‌War-goddess ​whose arrows ​decide ‌battles; ​her ​symbol ‌is ​the ‌crossed ​arrows ​on ​a ​shield.
- **Mother ‌of ‌the ​Gods** ‌— ​Sole ​parent ‌of ‌Sobek ‌in ‌the ​Fayum tradition; ‌in ​the ​Esna ​theology ‌she ​bears ​the ​sun.
- ‌**Lady ​of ​Sais** — ​Her ‌city ​in ‌the ​western ‌Delta ​held ‌her ‌great ​temple ​and the ​mysteries ​of ‌the ‌primeval ​waters.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Neith’s mythology ​is theology in ‌the superlative: she is ‌not a goddess ​within the pantheon ​but the condition of ​it. Her priesthood ​at Sais taught ​that she was self-generated, ‌that she wove ​the world, and ​that all gods were ‌her children — ​a doctrine so ‌old it survived ​into the latest periods ‌essentially unchanged.[^1]

### The ​Cow Who Bore ​the Sun (Esna Cosmogony)

​The great hymns ​of Esna make ​Neith the mother of ‌Ra: she as ​the celestial cow ‌gives birth to the ​sun-disc from between ‌her horns, and ​the seven scorpions ‌that escort Isis are ​her daughters. Creation ‌here is maternity ​on a cosmic scale ​— the goddess ‌is the source ‌from which the solar ‌order proceeds.[^2]

### Mother ​of Sobek (Fayum ​Theology)

In the crocodile-god’s ‌country, Neith is ​Sobek’s mother and ​the lady of ‌the deep waters he ​rises from. The ​pairing of a ‌primeval water-goddess with her ​crocodile son gives ‌the Fayum’s theology ​its structure: she is ​the *Nun*-like depth, ​he its dangerous, ​fertile emergence.

### The ‌Oracle of the Gods ‌(Contendings of Horus ​and Seth)

When ‌the divine tribunal deadlocked ​over the succession ​of Horus and ‌Seth, Neith was consulted ‌as the eldest ‌of counsel. Her ‌written oracle — quoted ​verbatim in the ‌New Kingdom narrative ​— demands the ​throne for Horus and ​compensation for Seth, ‌and threatens to ​make the sky fall ​if the gods ​disobey. They obeyed.

### ‌The Veiled Image of ​Sais (Greek Reportage)

​Plutarch preserves the ​mystery of her cult-image ‌at Sais: an ​image that was ‌never unveiled, before ​which stood the inscription ‌‘I am all ​that has been, ‌and is, and shall ‌be; and no ​mortal has ever ​lifted my veil.’ The ​*aisa*-mysteries of Sais ​entered the Hermetic ‌and Platonic imagination as ‌the emblem of ​unknowable first-nature.
